concepts.title: Supervised Learning
concepts.one_liner: Supervised learning is the process of observing example input-output behavior to infer a functional mapping that explains that behavior.
concepts.content:
Learning from examples is also called supervised learning. In this context, we are learning an algorithm, which is a computable mapping from inputs to outputs. A formal definition of an example is an {`input`, `output`} pair. For instance, a set of examples might consist of pairs such as:

$$\begin{aligned}
    &\{\texttt{input:} [2,3], \texttt{output:} 36\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} [7,1], \texttt{output:} 49\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} [5,2], \texttt{output:} 100\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} [2,2], \texttt{output:}16\}\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$

This kind of learning, where you observe example input-output behavior and infer a functional mapping that explains this behavior, is called supervised learning. Another name for this kind of learning is fitting a model to data.
concepts.motivation_md: Supervised learning allows us to automate decision-making by training algorithms on historical data where the correct answers are already known, enabling the model to predict outputs for new, unseen inputs.
concepts.recap_md: - Supervised learning involves inferring a functional mapping from provided input-output pairs.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Learning
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised learning involves finding useful representations or models of input data without being provided target outputs.
concepts.content: In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of input data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ but we are not told the target outputs $\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$. Instead, the learner has to come up with a model or representation of the input data that has useful properties, as measured by some objective function. The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: When labeled data is unavailable or expensive to obtain, unsupervised learning helps discover hidden patterns, structures, or efficient representations within raw data.
concepts.recap_md: - The learner is provided with input data but no corresponding target labels.

concepts.title: Reinforcement Learning
concepts.one_liner: Reinforcement learning is a framework where a learner seeks to maximize a reward function that measures the quality of its outputs.
concepts.content: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a reward function that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output. To be precise, a reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores: $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The learner tries to come up with a function that maximizes rewards. This kind of learning is becoming an important part of computer vision, especially in the context of vision for robots.
concepts.motivation_md: Reinforcement learning is essential for agents that must learn to make a sequence of decisions in an environment to achieve a goal, guided only by occasional feedback or rewards.
concepts.recap_md: - A reward function $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ maps outputs to numerical scores.

concepts.title: Key Ingredients of Learning
concepts.one_liner: A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients: an objective, a hypothesis space, and an optimizer.
concepts.content:
A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients:

1. Objective: What does it mean for the learner to succeed, or, at least, to perform well?
2. Hypothesis Space: What is the set of possible mappings from inputs to outputs that we will search over?
3. Optimizer: How, exactly, do we search the hypothesis space for a specific mapping that maximizes the objective?

These three ingredients, when applied to large amounts of data and run on sufficient hardware (referred to as compute), can do amazing things. A learner outputs an algorithm, $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, which maps inputs, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$, to outputs, $\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}$.

[FIGURE:606f041122e8e0fc | A learner outputs an algorithm f mapping inputs to outputs.]
concepts.motivation_md: Breaking down learning into these three components provides a structured framework for designing and analyzing any machine learning system.
concepts.recap_md: - The objective defines success, the hypothesis space defines possible models, and the optimizer defines the search method.

concepts.title: Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: A loss function is an objective that scores model outputs or compares them to target answers, typically to be minimized.
concepts.content: The objective that the learner optimizes is typically a function that scores model outputs, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or compares model outputs to target answers, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. We will interchangeably call this $\mathcal{L}$ either the objective function, the loss function, or the loss. A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to minimize, whereas an objective function can be used to describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.
concepts.motivation_md: Loss functions provide a mathematical way to quantify the error of a model, giving the optimizer a clear signal on how to improve the learned function.
concepts.recap_md: - A loss function $\mathcal{L}$ measures the discrepancy between model outputs and targets.

concepts.title: Importance of Parameterization
concepts.one_liner: To fully define a learning algorithm, one must specify both the hypothesis space and how that space is parameterized.
concepts.content: The hypothesis space can be described by a set $\mathcal{F}$ of all the possible functions under consideration by the learner. For example, one hypothesis space might be "all mappings from $\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$" and another could be "all functions $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ that satisfy the conditions of being a distance metric." Commonly, however, we will not just specify the hypothesis space, but also how we parameterize the space. For example, we may say that our parameterized hypothesis space is $y = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$, where $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ are the parameters. Another choice could be $y = \theta_2\theta_1 x + \theta_0$, with parameters $\theta_0$, $\theta_1$, and $\theta_2$. These two choices parameterize exactly the same space, meaning any affine function can be represented by either and both can only represent affine functions. However, these two parameterizations are not equivalent because optimizers and objectives may treat different parameterizations differently. Because of this, to fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.
concepts.motivation_md: Different parameterizations of the same set of functions can significantly affect how easily an optimizer can find the best solution.

concepts.title: Overparameterization
concepts.one_liner: Overparameterized models use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data.
concepts.content: Overparameterized models, where you use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data, are especially important in modern computer vision; most neural networks are overparameterized.
concepts.motivation_md: In modern deep learning, using more parameters than data points often leads to better generalization and easier optimization, contrary to classical statistical intuition.

concepts.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
concepts.one_liner: Cross-entropy loss is a continuous and differentiable function used to optimize classification models by maximizing the log likelihood of ground truth observations.
concepts.content:
Cross-entropy loss is commonly used because it is continuous and differentiable, making it easier to optimize than discrete alternatives. It is defined as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = H(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = - \sum_{k=1}^K y_k \log \hat{y}_k
\end{aligned}$$
In this context, $\hat{y}_k$ represents the probability the model assigns to class $k$. Under this interpretation, minimizing cross-entropy maximizes the log likelihood of the ground truth observation $\mathbf{y}$ under the model's prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard classification error is often NP-hard to optimize directly. Cross-entropy loss provides a smooth, differentiable surrogate that allows for efficient optimization via gradient-based methods while statistically maximizing the likelihood of the correct labels.
concepts.recap_md: - It is defined as the negative sum of ground truth labels multiplied by the log of predicted probabilities.

key_passage.text: $$\mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = H(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = - \sum_{k=1}^K y_k \log \hat{y}_k$$ The way to think about this is $\hat{y}_k$ should *represent the probability* we think the image is an image of class $k$. Under that interpretation, minimizing cross-entropy maximizes the log likelihood of the ground truth observation $\mathbf{y}$ under our model's prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.

concepts.title: Probability Mass Function (pmf)
concepts.one_liner: A probability mass function (pmf) is a $K$-dimensional vector with elements in the range $[0,1]$ that sum to 1.
concepts.content: For the interpretation of model outputs as probabilities to be valid, the prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ must represent a probability mass function (pmf). A pmf $\mathbf{p}$ over $K$ classes is defined as a $K$-dimensional vector with elements in the range $[0,1]$ that sums to 1. In other words, $\mathbf{p}$ is a point on the $(K-1)$-simplex, denoted as $\mathbf{p} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: To treat neural network outputs as probabilities, we need a mathematical structure that ensures the values are non-negative and represent a complete distribution over all possible outcomes.
concepts.recap_md: - A pmf must consist of values between 0 and 1 inclusive.

concepts.title: Simplex
concepts.one_liner: The $(K-1)$-simplex is the set of all $K$-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1.
concepts.content: The $(K-1)$-simplex, denoted $\vartriangle^{K-1}$, is the set of all $K$-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1. In the context of classification, $K$-dimensional one-hot codes live on the vertices of $\vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The simplex provides a geometric representation of the space of all possible probability distributions over a finite set of categories.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the space of all valid probability mass functions for $K$ classes.

concepts.title: Softmax Function
concepts.one_liner: The softmax function squashes a vector of real numbers into a probability distribution that sums to 1.
concepts.content:
To ensure that the output of a learned function $f_{\theta}$ is a valid probability mass function (i.e., $f_{\theta} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$), we can apply the softmax function. This involves two steps: first applying a function $z_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^K$, then squashing and normalizing the output. 

Using softmax is a modeling choice; any function that squashes into a valid pmf (a nonnegative vector that sums to 1) could be used. The function is defined as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    &\mathbf{z} = z_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\\
    &\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \texttt{softmax}(\mathbf{z})\\
    &\quad \quad \hat{y}_j = \frac{e^{-z_j}}{\sum_{i=1}^K e^{-z_k}}.
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Raw model outputs (logits) can be any real numbers. The softmax function maps these values into a range $[0, 1]$ and ensures they sum to 1, allowing them to be interpreted as probabilities.
concepts.recap_md: - It transforms arbitrary real-valued vectors into points on the simplex.

key_passage.text: A popular way to squash is via the softmax function: $\hat{y}_j = \frac{e^{-z_j}}{\sum_{i=1}^K e^{-z_k}}$.

concepts.title: Logits
concepts.one_liner: Logits are the unnormalized log probabilities of each class in a classification model.
concepts.content: The values in the vector $\mathbf{z}$ (the output of the model before the softmax function is applied) are called the logits. They can be interpreted as the unnormalized log probabilities of each class.
concepts.motivation_md: Logits provide a raw score for each class before normalization, which is often more numerically stable for certain calculations like loss functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Logits represent the input to the softmax function.

concepts.title: Softmax Regression
concepts.one_liner: Softmax regression is a family of learning methods that map input data to class labels using the softmax function and cross-entropy loss.
concepts.content:
Softmax regression is a family of learning methods for classification problems. It refers to the general form of mapping input data to class labels using a hypothesis space and an optimizer, typically involving the softmax function to produce class probabilities.

(see figure: Learning is a meta-algorithm, an algorithm that outputs algorithms; metalearning is just learning applied to learning, and therefore it is a meta-meta-algorithm.)

In this framework, the hypothesis space and optimizer are often left partially specified because softmax regression describes the whole family of methods sharing this structure. This modularity allows for developing the ingredients of the learning problem in isolation and then mixing and matching them.
concepts.motivation_md: Softmax regression generalizes binary logistic regression to multi-class problems, providing a standard framework for categorical prediction.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a general family of models for classification.

key_passage.text: Softmax regression is just one way to model a classification problem.

concepts.title: Metalearning (Learning to Learn)
concepts.one_liner: Metalearning, or learning to learn, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space consists of learning algorithms.
concepts.content:
Learning to learn, also called metalearning, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space is learning algorithms. While standard learners train on past instances to solve future instances, metalearning handles cases where the future problem is itself a learning problem, such as finding a least-squares line fit.

For example, given sets of input-output pairs that represent regression tasks:
$$\begin{aligned}
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[1,2]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = x\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[2,4]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = 2x\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[0.5,1]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = \frac{x}{2}\}\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$
A learner can fit these examples by learning to perform least-squares regression. Note that the metalearner might arrive at any solution that fits the examples well, not just the unique least-squares solution.

If learning is a meta-algorithm (an algorithm that outputs an algorithm), metalearning is a meta-meta-algorithm. It can be visualized by adding another outer loop on top of a learner.

(see figure: Learning is a meta-algorithm, an algorithm that outputs algorithms; metalearning is just learning applied to learning, and therefore it is a meta-meta-algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard learning algorithms are often hand-designed. Metalearning seeks to automate the discovery of learning algorithms, potentially finding more efficient ways to learn from small amounts of data.
concepts.recap_md: - It treats the process of learning itself as the task to be optimized.

concepts.title: Learning as a Meta-Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Learning is a meta-algorithm that extracts lessons from past experience to output an algorithm for solving future problems.
concepts.content:
The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past experience in order to solve future problems. Typically, this involves searching for an algorithm that solves past instances of the problem. This algorithm can then be applied to future instances of the problem. Past and future do not necessarily refer to the calendar date; instead they refer to what the learner has previously seen and what the learner will see next. Because learning is itself an algorithm, it can be understood as a meta-algorithm: an algorithm that outputs algorithms.

(see figure: Learning is an algorithm that outputs algorithms.)
concepts.motivation_md: Instead of manually hard-coding a solution for every specific problem, we use learning to automatically discover the best solution (an algorithm) based on available data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning is a meta-algorithm because its output is itself an algorithm.
 - It uses past experience (training data) to find a solution for future instances.
 - The 'past' and 'future' are defined by the learner's sequence of observations.

concepts.title: Training and Testing Phases
concepts.one_liner: Learning consists of a training phase to find a high-performing algorithm and a testing phase to solve new problem instances.
concepts.content: Learning usually consists of two phases: the training phase, where we search for an algorithm that performs well on past instances of the problem (training data), and the testing phase, where we deploy our learned algorithm to solve new instances of the problem.
concepts.motivation_md: To ensure that a learned solution actually works and hasn't just memorized specific examples, we must separate the process of finding the solution from the process of evaluating its performance on unseen data.
concepts.recap_md:
- The training phase involves searching for an algorithm using past data.
 - The testing phase evaluates the learned algorithm on new, unseen instances.
 - This separation is fundamental to assessing the generalization of a learner.

concepts.title: Empirical Risk Minimization

position.section_title: Empirical Risk Minimization: A Formalization of Learning from Examples

concepts.one_liner: Empirical Risk Minimization is a framework for supervised learning that aims to minimize the average error, or risk, over the training data.
concepts.motivation_md: In supervised learning, we need a formal way to select the 'best' hypothesis from a set of possibilities. ERM provides this by defining 'best' as the function that minimizes the average loss across our observed training examples, serving as a proxy for performance on unseen data.
concepts.recap_md: - ERM seeks to find a function $f$ in the hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ that minimizes the average loss over $N$ training samples.

key_passage.text: The idea is to minimize the average error (i.e., risk) we incur over all the training data (i.e., empirical distribution).

motivation.text: The three ingredients from the last section can be formalized using the framework of (ERM). This framework applies specifically to the supervised setting where we are learning a function that predicts y from x given many training examples.

concepts.title: Learning as Maximum Likelihood Inference
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood learning interprets ERM as inferring the hypothesis that assigns the highest probability to the observed training data.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides a probabilistic foundation for learning. By framing learning as maximizing the likelihood of the data, we can use the tools of statistics to justify specific loss functions and understand the uncertainty in our models.
concepts.recap_md: - Maximum likelihood learning selects the hypothesis $f$ that maximizes the probability of the observed outputs given the inputs.

key_passage.text: The term p(\{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N \bigm | \{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, f) is called the likelihood of the \mathbf{y} values given the model f and the observed \mathbf{x} values, and maximizing this quantity is called maximum likelihood learning.

motivation.text: Depending on the loss function, there is often an interpretation of ERM as doing maximum likelihood probabilistic inference. In this interpretation, we are trying to infer the hypothesis f that assigns the highest probability to the data.

concepts.title: Likelihood
concepts.one_liner: Likelihood is the probability of the observed output values given a specific model and the observed input values.

concepts.motivation_md: Likelihood quantifies how well a specific hypothesis or model explains the observed data, allowing us to compare different models based on their statistical fit.
concepts.recap_md: - Likelihood is defined as the conditional probability of the data given the model parameters or hypothesis.

concepts.title: Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) Learning
concepts.one_liner: Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) learning infers the most probable hypothesis given the training data by combining a likelihood function with a prior distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard maximum likelihood can sometimes lead to overfitting or pick hypotheses that are physically unrealistic. MAP learning allows us to incorporate prior knowledge or preferences (priors) into the learning process to regularize the result.
concepts.recap_md: - MAP learning finds the hypothesis $f$ that maximizes the posterior probability $p(f|data)$.

key_passage.text: When a prior is used in conjunction with a likelihood function, we arrive at maximum a posteriori learning (MAP learning), which infers the most probable hypothesis given the training data

concepts.title: Linear Least-Squares Regression
concepts.one_liner: Linear least-squares regression models the relationship between two variables by finding the best-fitting line through observed data points.
concepts.content:
One of the simplest learning problems is known as linear least-squares regression. In this setting, we aim to model the relationship between two variables, $x$ and $y$, with a line. For example, if $x$ represents the temperature outside and $y$ represents the number of people at the beach, we train our model on many observed examples of {`temperature outside`, `number of people at the beach`} pairs, denoted as $\{x^{(i)},y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. At test time, this model can be applied to predict the $y$ value of a new query $x'$, as shown in (see figure: The goal of learning is to use the training data to predict the $y$ value of the test query. In our example we find that for every 1 degree increase in temperature, we can expect $\sim 10$ more...).

Our hypothesis space consists of linear functions where the relationship between $x$ and our predictions $\hat{y}$ has the form $\hat{y} = f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$. This space is parameterized by two scalars, $\theta_0, \theta_1 \in \mathbb{R}$, representing the intercept and slope. Learning consists of finding the value of these parameters that maximizes the objective. The resulting $\theta^*$ defines the best fitting line to our data, which can be used to predict future observations (see figure: A best fit line is a visualization of a function $f_{\theta}$, that predicts the $y$-value for each input $x$-value.).

The entire linear least-squares learning problem is summarized in (see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.). In these diagrams, the objective $J(\theta)$ is understood to imply $J(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear regression is a fundamental tool for predicting a continuous outcome based on an input variable. It provides a simple, interpretable model for understanding how changes in one variable correlate with another.

Learning consists of finding the value of these parameters that maximizes the objective.

concepts.title: Program Induction
concepts.one_liner: Program induction is a broad class of learning algorithms where the hypothesis space consists of computer programs, such as all possible Python programs.
concepts.content: Program induction is one of the broadest classes of learning algorithm. In this setting, our hypothesis space may be all Python programs. Unlike linear least-squares, where the learned function is an algebraic expression mapping $x$ to $y$ via two scalar parameters $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ (see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.), program induction searches for a Python program that maps $x$ to $y$ (see figure: Python program induction finds a Python program that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.). Learning consists of searching over the space of all possible Python programs (within some max length), which is a much harder search problem than finding two scalars.
concepts.motivation_md: While linear models are simple, many real-world processes are better described by complex logic or algorithms. Program induction allows for a much more flexible hypothesis space that can represent any computable function.
concepts.recap_md: - Program induction uses a hypothesis space of computer programs rather than simple mathematical functions.

key_passage.text: In this setting, our hypothesis space may be all Python programs. In this case, the learned function is a Python program that maps x to y. Learning consisted of searching over the space of all possible Python programs (within some max length).

concepts.title: One-Hot Code
concepts.one_liner: A one-hot code is a vector representation for class labels where only one element is set to 1 and all others are 0.
concepts.content:
A convenient representation for class labels is to let $\mathbf{y}$ be a $K$-dimensional vector, for $K$ possible classes, with $y_k = 1$ if $\mathbf{y}$ represents class $k$, and $y_k = 0$ otherwise. This representation is called a one-hot code, since just one element of the vector is on ("hot"). Each class has a unique one-hot code. These codes serve as the targets for the function we are learning. Our goal is to learn a function $f_{\theta}$ that outputs vectors $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ that match the one-hot codes, thereby correctly classifying the input images. 

An example of one-hot codes for representing $K$=5 different classes:

[FIGURE:b8af1eed48fae94a]
concepts.motivation_md: Categorical labels (like 'cat' or 'dog') cannot be used directly in mathematical optimization. One-hot encoding converts these labels into numerical vectors, allowing models to calculate loss and gradients for classification tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - One-hot encoding represents $K$ classes as $K$-dimensional vectors with a single 1 and $K-1$ zeros.

concepts.title: 0-1 Loss
concepts.one_liner: The 0-1 loss is a loss function that evaluates to 1 for any misclassification and 0 for a correct prediction.
concepts.content:
The 0-1 loss is a loss function used to minimize misclassifications. It is defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = \mathbb{1}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\neq\mathbf{y}),
\end{aligned}
$$ 

where $\mathbb{1}$ is the indicator function that evaluates to 1 if and only if its argument is true, and 0 otherwise.
concepts.motivation_md: In classification, we often care most about the total number of errors. The 0-1 loss directly counts these errors, providing a simple metric for accuracy, though it is difficult to optimize directly because it is not differentiable.
concepts.recap_md: - 0-1 loss assigns a penalty of 1 for an incorrect prediction and 0 for a correct one.

key_passage.text: Our first idea might be that we should minimize misclassifications. That would correspond to the so called 0-1 loss: $\mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = \mathbb{1}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\neq\mathbf{y})$, where $\mathbb{1}$ is the indicator function that evaluates to 1 if and only if its argument is true, and 0 otherwise.

prereq.rationale: Supervised learning involves a training phase where the mapping is inferred from examples and a testing phase where the mapping is applied.
The training and testing phases are the standard procedural decomposition of the learning meta-algorithm.
Unsupervised learning is a specific paradigm of the general learning meta-algorithm.
Reinforcement learning is a specific framework for learning functions through optimization.
The key ingredients provide the structural components for the learning meta-algorithm previously introduced.
The loss function is a specific, common implementation of the 'Objective' ingredient in a learning algorithm.
The learned function is defined as the specific output produced by the learner using its three ingredients.
Parameterization is a practical method for defining and restricting the 'Hypothesis Space' ingredient.
Overparameterization is defined in terms of using more parameters than necessary within a parameterized hypothesis space.
Metalearning specifically defines its hypothesis space as a set of learning algorithms.
Evolution is identified as a learning algorithm based on the meta-algorithm definition established in this chapter.
ERM is specifically defined as a framework for the supervised learning setting where functions are learned from input-output pairs.
The ERM objective function is defined as the average of a loss function over the training set.
ERM involves searching over a hypothesis space to find the function that minimizes empirical risk.
Linear least-squares regression is a fundamental example of supervised learning where a model is trained on observed input-output pairs.
One-hot codes are a standard representation for discrete class labels used as targets in supervised classification tasks.
The softmax function is specifically used to transform a vector of real numbers into a valid probability mass function.
Logits are defined as the unnormalized values produced by a model immediately before the softmax function is applied.
Softmax regression relies on the softmax function to map internal model outputs to class probabilities.
Softmax regression typically uses cross-entropy loss to optimize the parameters of the classification model.
Maximum likelihood learning is presented as a specific probabilistic interpretation of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM).
The probabilistic interpretation of learning as maximum likelihood depends on the specific loss function being used.

overlay.rationale: Supervised learning is a specific paradigm of the general learning meta-algorithm where the learning process is guided by explicit input-output examples.
Unsupervised learning is defined by the absence of the target outputs that characterize supervised learning.
Reinforcement learning uses a scalar reward signal to evaluate outputs rather than the explicit target outputs used in supervised learning.
Reinforcement learning relies on external feedback (rewards), whereas unsupervised learning focuses on internal data structure without external signals.
Metalearning is defined as a special case of learning where the hypothesis space consists of learning algorithms rather than simple mappings.
The text uses the task of finding a least-squares line fit as a concrete example of a problem a metalearner might solve.
ERM provides the mathematical structure that combines the key ingredients of learning—data, loss, and hypothesis space—into an optimization problem.
Linear least-squares is a classic application of empirical risk minimization, finding parameters that minimize the error on training data.
Program induction involves searching a much more complex hypothesis space (computer programs) than the scalar parameters used in linear regression.
The 0-1 loss is a specific type of loss function used to evaluate misclassifications in discrete settings.
Cross-entropy is a continuous and differentiable loss function used for optimizing classification models.
Minimizing cross-entropy loss is mathematically equivalent to maximizing the log likelihood of the ground truth observations.
One-hot codes can be viewed as a specific type of PMF where the probability mass is concentrated entirely on a single class.
